A review of the new $ 249 Google Chrome Book

Google has introduced a new portable computer - they call it the perfect additional computer - and I see it as a paradigm shift in the role of a portable computing device.

The new Samsung Chrome Book has an 11.6-inch full color display. It weights 2.42 lbs and is .7 inches thin. It has a battery life of over 6.5 hours and runs on a Samsung Dual processor with 100 GB of online Google Drive space. It features a web cam with USB and HDMI ports and is Bluetooth compatible. It runs the Chrome OS, which means it has Google apps built in, and is priced at $249.

I think it's one of the most remarkable product introductions I've seen in my 35 years working in the PC industry.

This new Chrome Book re-defines what a portable computer can do and how it can be used, and is completely based on the concept of Cloud Computing . It works right out of the box, has no moving parts, and has built-in anti-virus protection.

Google has created a complete infrastructure for cloud computing; Google Chrome browser for surfing the web, Google email, online google docs application software compatible with MS Office apps, google drive to store whatever documents you want in the cloud, free downloadable apps such as google voice for phone calls and video conferencing with webcam, and dozens of other applications. And of course the Google Search Engine. All the software you need is in the Google Cloud.

I've had 5 portable computers over the years and I bought each one to be an additional computer to my office computers. But now you don't need a bulky expensive laptop computer with a big hard disk and Microsoft Office installed on it.

I had also bought an IPad as a possible new portable computing device. Trying to use my Ipad for email and type on the glass was maddening. I couldn't get it to print as I didn't have an Apple Airprint compatible printer, and I was shocked to learn that I could only buy music and media through Apple Itunes.

I could easily print to any of my printers with the Chrome Book, it has a great real keyboard, and I can buy anything from anywhere - Amazon or whatever vendor I can get the best prices from.
Placed side by side, The Macbook Air and The Google Chrome Book look almost like twins in design, keyboard and screen size.

With the Chrome Book, I can surf the web, watch Youtube videos, play games, check my email, video chat, make free phone calls, and If I want to create a letter or a spreadsheet I just use Google docs and I can store them online in Google drive. If there are files on my main computers I want to be able to access with my Chrome Book, I can upload those files to my online Google drive, and be able to access and edit them.

The new Samsung Chrome Book defines the new world of Cloud Computing and provides virtually everyone easy access to this world at an astoundingly low price. I also feel that many people could use this as their only computing device.

Even the Kindle reading app that I've been using for years crashed on a regular basis. Motorola was a decent company until Chinese Lenova bought it. Now all their products are crap. They need to fire their entire engineering staff and start again from scratch. Samsung only for me from now on.

The G6 is a good phone for the price so long as you're realistic and don't try to compare it to a $900 flagship phone from another brand. For $299 (or barely more than half that when it goes on sale), you are getting a 6+ inch 1080p screen, 4 gigs of RAM, and 64 gigs of internal storage with the ability to add more via a micro SD card slot. It will work on pretty much any carrier (GSM or CDMA), the battery will get you through a work day, and while it only has one speaker, it still is pretty loud compared to many. I'll just toss a few highlight of my own in since it's already been reviewed by tons of people:

PRO: Good screen though not as bring as the G5 for comparison. 70% on this = 50% on the older G5, but still ok once you crank it up.

PRO: Cameras are not great, but good. HDR is improved over past models, detail if more than fine enough for social media and 4x6 prints. The portrait mode (background blur) could be improved but works MOST of the time.

PRO: Call reception at least in my area is good. Decent speaker and headphone jack lets you use corded headsets.

CON: Wifi can sometimes kick off and you have to re-connect it. Random and not often, but worth watching.

CON: No NFC, meaning if you want to store a credit card in it to wave over store terminals to pay for something, you're out of luck. It's turned on with the European models of this, but off on U.S. models (Booooo Moto).

CON: Moto slow with Android updates. This comes with Android 9.0 - expect maybe one major update and a few security updates over 2 years (or so) and that's it.

CON: Has a glass back but no wireless charging, so, it's fragile. Get a good case and use screen protectors.

So again - this is NOT an $800-$1,000 phone, but it comes ridiculously close to most of their features for one-third the price. I think for many people if they spent some time with this, they'd find it suits their needs just as well and could save some money. Look for sales.

For the price, this is a great Chromebook. It checks a lot of boxes and I've done my fair share of research.

1. Solid build. Nice sturdy plastic chassis. (Keeps it lightweight)
2. USB type C port, SD card slot, HDMI, and USB 3.0
3. Touchscreen with an IPS display
4. 4 gigs of RAM and 64gig of storage. (rare at this price point)
5. Nice feel to the keyboard and track pad.
6. ARM processor that is optimized for the Google play store apps and runs much better than the Intel celerons you see in most low-end Chromebooks.

You get a lot for $300. You can't really find those options within that price range. The only thing I wish it had was a FHD display. 1366x768 still looks sharp on an 11.6 in screen but it would be super sharp if it was 1080p. I would highly recommend this Chromebook.

So I'm a busy college student who who was looking for a laptop that wouldn't cost me a fortune. Being a student, I was looking for something that was easy to throw in my backpack, had a long battery life, and was easy to take notes with (with a word processor or slide presentation). After having the Samsung Chromebook for about a week, I have to say that so far I'm really impressed.

Specifically, I've been really impressed with how the Chromebook has performed. I've been carrying it around in my backpack and have used it during all of my lectures. The battery lasts a lot longer than I was expecting, even with the screen set on the highest brightness setting, the battery has lasted the entire school day (around 5-6 hours).

Keep in mind that for $230, you have to sacrifice a few things. There is very little internal memory, but with Google Drive and/or a flash drive, this is something that shouldn't be a deal breaker. Also, it does take a little bit of time to get used to the Google operating system if you haven't used it before, but after only a week I already am feeling pretty comfortable with it. I have used Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Calender for a few years now, so the transition was pretty smooth. If you aren't very well acquainted with these Google products, then this product might not be for you since it is powered by these apps.

If you are a hardcore gamer, photographer, or are into some other computer-dependent hobby, then be weary of buying a Chromebook since a lot of games/programs that you may want to download might not be compatible with a Chrome Operating system.

The take home message: if you consider yourself somewhat tech savvy and don't mind getting used to a new operating system, then get the Samsung Chromebook! I am very happy with my purchase and don't have any regrets!

Keep in mind that for $230, you have to sacrifice a few things. There is very little internal memory, but with Google Drive and/or a flash drive, this is something that shouldn't be a deal breaker. Also, it does take a little bit of time to get used to the Google operating system if you haven't used it before, but after only a week I already am feeling pretty comfortable with it. I have used Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Calender for a few years now, so the transition was pretty smooth. If you aren't very well acquainted with these Google products, then this product might not be for you since it is powered by these apps.

If you are a hardcore gamer, photographer, or are into some other computer-dependent hobby, then be weary of buying a Chromebook since a lot of games/programs that you may want to download might not be compatible with a Chrome Operating system.

The take home message: if you consider yourself somewhat tech savvy and don't mind getting used to a new operating system, then get the Samsung Chromebook! I am very happy with my purchase and don't have any regrets!

I also helped my buddy set up his phone, and he runs Windows 10, and this phone connected just fine to that as well.

Now that the price on this phone has gone down to $600, it is a very good deal for the price.

The Snapdragon 865 processor is more than fast enough for anything I want to do. 6GB of memory is less than some other phones in this price range, but it is still more than enough for most people.

The phone feels very solid despite the plastic back. If you use any kind of case, you won't even notice the plastic back.

The phone supports 25W fast charging, but for some reason they only included a 15W charger in the box. Buying the 25W charger separately is a waste of money as well as a waste of the natural resources that were used on the 15W charger. Amazon sells decent 25W fast chargers for less than $15, so cheaping out on the charger is a real lame move by Samsung. You can search Amazon for 15W chargers that support "USB-C PPS" mode and are UL Certified.

The screen looks beautiful when you turn on the 120Hz mode. This does burn your battery more quickly, but the battery is big enough that it still lasts all day.

The screen has been very responsive to me. I have read bug reports about screen glitches for some people. Samsung has already released bug fixes that hopefully have fixed this. I advise only buying this phone from an authorized dealer with no hassle returns so you don't have to worry about this bug.

The phone does have a lot of Samsung bloatware. I owned a Samsung S-series phone several years ago and the bloatware was really bad then. This one is much better. You don't even need to create a Samsung account to use the phone now. Most of the Samsung bloatware (other than the camera app) won't work if you don't have a Samsung account, but if you never use it, this isn't a problem. There are several tutorials online about disabling all the bloatware if you never want to see any of it on your screen.

The triple camera setup on this phone is very good for this price level. The telephone camera works great up to 3X in good light. Image quality deteriorates quickly if you zoom in past 3X or in lower lighting conditions. Telephoto cameras are getting rare in this smartphone price range, so I'm glad this phone has one. I really like using the telephoto lens for landscape and nature photography. The normal and wide angle cameras work better in lower light situations (including indoor situations), though not as good as the iphone or Google Pixel phones. Pictures do tend look more processed than with some other phone cameras. Some people like the Samsung look. Other people prefer more natural looking photos. You should try to look at sample photos before buying the phone, since you cannot completely disable the Samsung photo processing.

This phone comes with Android version 10 out of the box, which is one version behind the Android version 11 that the Google Pixel phones are shipping with. Samsung promises software support with 3 version updates, but that is a little misleading since 1 of those version updates will be just to catch up with the current Android version 11. Still, 3 years of bug fixes and security patches is better than what Samsung used to offer.

A bit of background on myself: I'm a devoted and longtime Mac user, and I work at a website development company. I consider myself quite computer literate. I own a Macbook Pro but it's about 3 years old now, and the battery is getting pretty crappy so I can't bring it anywhere without needing a charge after about 1.5 hours. I could either buy a new battery for $200 or get a Chromebook for $250, I chose the latter. I'm a student as well, so having a very portable machine is important. With all that said, the Chomebook is awesome! When I'm not working (writing code, using lots of computing power) the Chromebook is perfect for all of my needs. Honestly, about 99% of people who use computers only use them for two things: internet related activities, and word processing/spreadsheets, the exact two things that the Chromebook does best. I feel that cloud based machines like this are the future of computing. There is a misconception that your abilities are severely limited by the cloud based OS, but it's really not true. This computer is shockingly lightweight and thin, while the keyboard and trackpad are more than adequate. I would recommend buying an SD card along with this, just to make sure you have some extra storage if needed. I could rave about this for days, but the bottom line is: it's a perfect second computer for those like me, and it would make a perfect first computer for just about anyone who isn't in a computer-related field of work.

I'm also seriously considering dual-booting Ubuntu on this, but I'm gonna enjoy Chrome OS for a while :)

I never thought I would buy a laptop with no hard drive. I did. And it's wonderful. The Chromebook made by Samsung is light - about 2.4 pounds, thin and has a 6.5-hour battery that pretty much is exactly that. And it boots up in 10 seconds. And it performs all the primary functions of a laptop – email, chat, word processing, etc. And performs them well.

The catch: You have to like Google products. A lot. The Chromebook has no hard drive, just a small flash memory with room for it’s Google operating system (similar to Android) and any of the apps you choose from the small list available. So everything you do has to be done via the Cloud. Specifically Google Docs, Spreadsheet and Presentation — now all part of Google Drive. Music and Photos can be enjoyed through the machine once added to Google+ or Drive.

The other catch is it is largely a WIFI machine. You can link it by wire to your internet modem and there is a 3G/WIFI version but if you have WIFI in the house or visit Starbucks, McDonalds or live in a digitally connected town, it works wonderfully. I don’t do a lot of heavy lifting on the computer – don’t crunch numbers, don’t play involved games, etc. Just email, browse and write. And this is a laptop that fits those needs.

The best catch: It cost $249.

Inconsistent battery life /charging speeds - when I first got this, we're talking 19 hours of me using it. That was impressive. Screen on time in the 6+ hour range, I could kill it if I tried but I'm a psycho power user. Somewhere around month 2 that dropped to finding myself needing to charge after I got home from work, where I wasn't using it.

Your battery life is screen on time, power used to do WiFi or Cell transmission and how much of that you're actually doing, whether you're actually doing anything. Battery should have been nearly full.

Cut to this past week, right back to all day power, with standard usage. Nothing tends to show in the battery usage summary, due to my rather unexciting life I'm usually in the same two places so it's not like I'm dealing with a lot of variables here. Something's up with their power management and here's the other thing I didn't mention - my wife has the same phone. The same issues popped up on hers and we don't really share software in common other than the basic Samsung and Google sets that come preinstalled.

Probably firmware as no battery usage for apps seemed untoward.

Next, this "cinema quality" 8K advertising nonsense. Nah, this is quite a few more pixels than that. 8K is surprisingly not a good experience. You'll be shooting it and it's jerky to watch on screen while shooting, and the end results are - they're good, but looking closely it's just better than 4K, not a whole lot clearer, not a whole lot of effective pixel addition. The codec seems to be set at "awww, they're never going to notice that" as opposed to "save all the image datas!"

Absolutely great phone, second Android phone I've had that I've had no desire to root it.

I will point out the one complaint I have here is Samsung support is completely useless - something's wrong with my wife's account and they refuse to read a ticket I put in about it - they see that I have an account, skip over all the words I wasted time writing that explained in complete detail what is wrong, and copy and paste how to log into my account.

No Samsung, for some reason her account doesn't work, her birthday claims it's incorrect so you refuse to send a password reset link or text message... this is the problem, not that me, the husband, has an account and can't log in....

I bought this phone specifically for the 10x optical zoom camera. This phone is actually really good and the physical hardware is great except for one major flaw. The camera software.

It applies SO MUCH extreme over-sharpening and noise reduction that I have to scale the image down to about 20% scale for it to not look like crap, and even then, some artifacts from the extreme over-sharpening are still visible. As a result, it is incapable of capturing fine details. Also it over-saturates photos a rather extreme amount. And on top of all of that, it saves as somewhat low quality jpegs. Everything about the photos the camera takes is extreme. Extreme zoom, extreme resolution, and extremely crappy.

If you want this phone for everything else it offers, then it's great. It just does a really bad job at taking photos compared to every other smart phone I've had in the past even though none of those phones had optical zoom and only had 8MP or less cameras.

edit: I've since bought a Pixel 5 Pro. Even though it's zoom is only 4x instead of 10x, it doesn't destroy the photos it takes with insane post processing, so it actually manages to capture more detail with only 4x optical zoom than this phone does at 10x optical zoom.

OK, so I purchased this phone because of the camera. I had read so much about it and for the first time in forever I was tempted to change from my 3rd edition of the Galaxy 7 Active (I have replaced mine 3 times because I like that phone so much as it has actual buttons so there is a smaller chance of inadvertently hitting the screen and initiating an unintended action and will hold up to my actions). That phone took really good photos, but it still couldn't come close to my 35mm camera. This one does and it has options unheard of in a SLR camera.
The photos attached are a great example. If you have had puppies you know how absolutely difficult it is to get a photo because they move so much and so quickly. With this camera...er phone....it takes about 10 frames before the shutter is engaged so even if he moved, I was able to go through the frames and select the one that got him before he moved. The first photo was the beauty shot that I wouldn't have had as he moved right as I clicked the shutter. I was able to get it from reviewing the motion photo and the frames right before I clicked. Similarly without that option I wouldn't have captured photos 2 or 3 or 4 as he was in motion as I shot every single one of those photos. How many times have you said, rats he moved when taking a photo? Particularly if you are shooting animals or children you know you are just as likely to miss the great shot you see in your lens because in the second it takes you to react and shoot, they move. Whoever came up with this motion photo that captures a bunch of frames before you click is a genius.
I have started watching YouTube videos because this camera is in many ways a completely new and different way of taking photos and video. Oh and if you want to select a frame from your video and turn that into a jpeg photo, you can do so.
I am really excited to take my walks this summer. I love macro shots of flowers and bugs, as well as sky shots when a storm is coming in. I typically select the best 10 or so shots taken over the summer in my daily walks to share with others in the area. With this phone I should have even better results. I won't have to go into the neighbor's yards to get up close vegetation shots as the zoom on this is unreal.
I find I use my phone more and more as a substitute for a tablet and with this phone I can see that I may do so by choice. It may be primarily intended to make phone calls but for most the functions are so good that it may do far, far more than that.
The pen and a case with a thick edge are absolute necessities. It is so much easier to navigate the page with the pen and with the pen you don't leave fingerprints. As I am using the screen to review photos, keeping it clean is a must. I have had Samsung pens come with a Chromebook and wasn't impressed, but with this one you will need to watch a separate video on just the functionality of the pen.
A case is needed both to stop inadvertent clicks as your fingers curve around the phone holding it and to enable you to hold it more steady when shooting photos/videos. I tried it without the case and it was a bust. I have nerve damage and can't feel the ends of 5 of my fingers and have nasty arthritis on top of that. The case will also protect the phone when I drop it and I will drop it, that is a given. Holding the phone resulted in numerous inadvertent clicks around the edge. There is an app you can download to create an edge border that will not be effected by touch but I would rather keep the edges as is and grab hold of a case. (I tried the app and it did help, but I felt it took up to much of that beautiful display).
I would also recommend a screen protector. It seems like a no brainer to me as screen breakage is the number one needed repair to cell phones and even with gorilla glass if you are constantly carrying this, getting it in and out, etc. you are going to strike that screen.
Oh and the camera makes good calls as well.....I mean the phone does!
I will update later, but if you are a novice there are a ton of YouTube how to videos available to teach you how to operate this and I would recommend that you go for it, particularly if you are like me a lover of photography. With this phone Samsung has truly changed the way you can obtain high quality images as well as providing a fantastic editing program to work with after you take the shot.

I have both a Samsung and Acer C7 Chromebook.

Samsung Pros:
*Awesome speakers. Very loud and true to music. Sounds like Bose. I can hear it across the room.
*Boots in 6 secs
*Long battery life
*Solid state, no fan - quiet and doesn't get hot
Cons:
*Keyboard doesn't have Del, Home, End, Page Up/Down keys

Acer C7 Pros:
*Love the keyboard layout
*A little less expensive than Samsung
*Has port for extra monitor.
Cons:
*Speakers suck. Even at highest volume, can barely hear out of them. Sounds tin-ny, like they are the lowest grade computer speakers.
*Boots in 8 secs
*A little heavier than Samsung
*Battery doesn't last as long (4 hours vs 6 hours)

All in all, I love both my Chromebooks. For everyday, I use the Acer because of the keyboard. For movies, webcam, videos, I use the Samsung.
I only use my windows based laptop for printing, external harddrive, etc. since its my "base" and I don't move it around the house. (Note Google has a cloud base print service for free. I use that to print when I'm on my chromebooks.)
I use the Chromebooks 99% of the time and am thinking of switching out my Windows laptop with the Acer due to the extra video port. I wish the Samsung had a better keyboard layout else I would say only get the Samsung. If not having a home/end/delete/page up/down doesn' bother you, just get the Samsung.
Note: The OS is Chrome, not Windows...and it plays everything Netflix, Hulu, etc.

What a disappointment! My first Motorola phone in years have let me down.

Let's talk about the pros:

1) Decent small bezel screen with good resolution, 18:9 ratio is chic!

2) Almost stock Android experience, if vanilla is your favorite flavor.

3) Built in Amazon Apps can be disabled, like you won't know it's there.

4) The Moto gestures are cool, you can activate camera app by twisting your hand twice while holding the phone. Make a chopping motion twice activates flash light. And you can use the fingerprint sensor to navigate the phone instead of your usual on screen buttons.

5) A turbo charger is included, you can charge your phone in under an hour from 0 to 100 easily. But I think I know why it has one bundled with it...Keep reading...

Moving on to the cons, oh boy it's a long one:

1) This is the LOW-SPEC version, other market gets 4gb of ram and 64gb of storage, as well as actual glass back. This one gets 3gb/32gb and a plastic build. Yuck!

2) This phone will only get one more major Android release, the current 8.0 operating system is soooooooooooo damn slow on this phone. Like it becomes sluggish once you have a few apps open. It reminds me of using earlier Android phones. Ah, the nostalgia!

3) Camera sucks despite being a "now in season" dual cam setup. And here are MULTIPLE REASONS WHY IT SUCKS.

A, The Moto camera app takes forever to take a picture.

B, It doesn't have OIS, so all your pictures WILL be blurry. You better be steady like you have three legs (like a tripod).

C, The stock Google photo app takes FOREVER to open the picture you've just taken. Vanilla is not always good!

D, The pictures taken by default tend to be oversaturated, everyone look like they have an orange tan. As my friend puts it, the way this camera renders color is like a flip phone from the early 2000s. UNACCEPTABLE!

4) This one nails it in the coffin, the BATTERY LIFE IS APPALLING! The battery barely lasts a day, even if you use it lightly over time, like just checking emails and using uber apps. I usually unplug my phone at 7AM, and by 2PM I find myself having to reach for the charger. Charging the phone slowly using a standard USB charger does make the battery last a smidge longer. However, I now know why it came with a turbo charger, because you'll be needing to charge this phone quite frequently!

In conclusion,
DON'T BUY THIS PHONE if you have other choices, a similarly priced Huawei or Nokia will perform better than this fraud of a Motorola (Hint: It's actually made by lenovo, which sucks at making phones if you don't already know).

I paid a few bucks more to purchase from Chubbiestech based on a review and to avoid any problems. (Reading about the A10 reviews was scaring me until I realized I was reading the wrong product lol.) This is for the Samsung Galaxy S10e. Being from the S- product line, it's Samsung's flagship product and you can read the history and differences between the models on Wikipedia. I found this information very helpful.

I lucked out with the right Seller and got a phone that really seems brand new and works excellent in every way. (A previous purchase of a different model and seller was excellent in every way but then we discovered it wouldn't charge.) I'm so happy I bought this!

Pros

Mine was in new condition without a scratch, and functions perfectly in every way. I was able to load SmartSwitch on my old J7 and only had to manually download a matching icon set (and create a new Samsung account to download it.) Everything else (including my custom wallpaper from an outside source) transferred exactly.

I wanted a smaller profile/screen because I really loved my J7 and can easily operate it with one hard. I find modern phones too large and heavy and I'm not a gamer. The S10e's profile is surprisingly *smaller* than the J- series and fit my desire. Could easily fit inside a shirt pocket.

It runs way faster than my old phone and I verified with DevCheck that it does indeed have 6 Gigs of Ram. That's more than I ever had before and so it seems real speedy and capable to me and also 128 Gigs of space is way more than I ever thought of using.

I mostly only use my phone as a music source and the sound quality thru my headphones is superb, like my J7 which I prefer to the modern soundboards that I have to tweak; I don't have to use the equalizer on this and the bass is great.

The Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, screentouch and call quality (and charging) all work great. The mobile data connection on my old sim for some reason is much faster (30M??) on 4GLTE and the upload speed is 3x my old phone too, I can't imagine why. But the connection with the same service is just stronger and has much better coverage. I didn't realize it was the old phone limiting it. That's like broadband over 4G lol.

I simply slipped in my old Sim and it connected with no problem or troubleshooting.

Anyway the S- series hardware of this phone is superb. Mine came with Android 12 which I understand is the highest available for this model. My J7 was stuck in Android 8. I didn't want to upgrade to a phablet nor pay a lot for features I didn't want to begin with.

Caveats/Tips

I never used a case before but this phone is so small (yay!) AND slippery I needed to buy a case. Don't want to drop it and scratch the screen because my big clumsy fingers can't hold onto it. I don't have a problem navigating the screensize.

Had to manually customize icons after installing everything. This requires a Samsung account. (You can delete it from Accounts afterward if you wish.)

If you use Smart Switch to transfer and duplicate your experience from your old phone you need to unpair the devices listed under Bluetooth and re-pair them for them to work on your new phone.

Many/Most of your programs transferred and websites will require you to log-in again (so you'll need your passwords) but the data (pics/docs/program files) transferred without a hitch. (You can download Smart Switch on your old phone from Google Play.)

My phone has the annoying T-mobile start-up screen (less annoying if you turn the sound off) but it doesn't harm anything functionally.

Samsung apps preinstalled cannot be uninstalled or disabled. However Google apps can be.

The battery is small (3100) but I'm used to that from the J7. I tried a larger capacity battery in my J7 but became impatient with the charging time so actually prefer the quick charging of these.

This review is obviously for folks who may not have done this before or are doubtful about the quality of the renewed product.

I'm totally happy with the new phone and the process of setting it up was seamless. Definitely worth it and you saved a lot of money! (Now you can peruse the internet and modern apps like the Joneses! :)

Update: It's a bit too small to be honest, and very SLIPPERY, however still prefer this to the large ones. Wish they still made J-size. But everything works great, sounds great and I'm getting 50M download on LTE! All I do is listen to music so it's fine for my needs. Great price for a fast phone.

I bought this in a hurry when my old Dell laptop died right before school started and this was all I could afford. It's worth what I paid, which is to say it's not worth a lot, but it works. Altogether, it's fine, but I wouldn't buy it again if I had the money to buy a non-Chromebook. I knew I'd suffer a little for the Chrome OS, but I didn't realize just how much because I'm not tech-savvy. I find it's pretty limited in what it can do (especially regarding schoolwork) but it covers the essentials acceptably, which is really all I should expect from a $220 machine.

Pros:

-The lack of startup time is fantastic! Being able to open it up and have it going in 10 seconds is really, really great. I was used to taking 5+ minutes just to get on my e-mail with my old dying Dell laptop.
-Lightweight and sleek; easy to transport; great for bringing to class
-good battery life
-questionably powerful enough for my needs, but not for my wants (see below)
-durable (?)

Cons:

-After almost 6 months of use, the performance seems to be getting progressively worse. When I first got it, things ran amazingly smoothly. I could have 8 tabs open (facebook, Youtube in the background, a document, buzzfeed articles queued up) and nothing would stutter and it all loaded quickly. Not anymore. Even simple pages can take forever to load. Sometimes, it works perfectly fine and other times, it's hardly functional. Closing superfluous tabs doesn't help-- it can run just as slow on a single pdf as it does with 7 buzzfeed articles open. I have these problems both running it on my home internet and school internet. Ultimately, the internet always works but it's just ridiculously slow sometimes. I would summarize the performance as being wildly inconsistent.

-It seems to run worse when it's not plugged in.

-Google Docs is awful on in its own right and the machine can barely run it. It stutters incessantly (possibly due to the constant auto-saving?) and it's basically impossible to make a well-organized, attractive document in Docs on a Chromebook. Skydrive (online MS Office) is not much better considering the Chrome OS limitations and the auto-saving. In either of these word processors, the lag is unbearable. If I need to type more than one page, it's literally less of a hassle for me to travel to school/stay later to do assignments than it is to produce them on the Chromebook. I have a >50-page document due at the end of every semester and I would rather eat my own tongue than attempt to even OPEN it on my Chromebook, let alone type it up.

-Don't even get me started on opening/trying to edit MS Word docs on a Chromebook. It opens in a program called QuickOffice which is awful. Documents are ugly and the formatting is ruined. Normally crashes if I try to edit them. One time, it crashed every time I hit the left shift key. Other times (95% of the time), it just crashes out of nowhere.

-You cannot use any Apple or Microsoft software. Considering that the world runs on these companies, this is a MAJOR drawback of the Chromebook. I had no idea it'd be this inconvenient. I can't use my school-specific software, watch some required videos, run some required software,or create and/or reasonably edit MS Office things.

-On that note, you need an app for EVERYTHING. If it's not a website, you probably need an app.

-The plastic shell feels kind of flimsy, especially around the trackpad. Sitting it on top of soft things (ex your knee, laptop sleeve) seems to screw up clicking-- almost like you could click by pressing on the underside of the shell under the trackpad. If you press on the shell next to the trackpad, you can see the whole keyboard rock. Still, like I said above, it does seem durable. Honestly, I've been known to slam the heel of my hand down on the trackpad/hand rest part when I get upset and it hasn't shown any signs of wear and tear. After almost 6 months, the plastic casing on the back of the keyboard part, like where all the ports are, is coming off. It clicks back on but I'm afraid of that the consequence will be if I can't put it back on someday. I've never dropped this thing or banged it off something, so I don't know why it's coming off.

-It sometimes ignores my clicks? I feel like sometimes (by that I mean daily, just not every time) I have to click on things multiple times in order for the Chromebook to register it. No signs of loading, etc-- just it acting as if I never clicked at all.

So, in summary, I wouldn't buy this Chromebook again if I had other options, but it'll do until I can afford to replace it with a Windows machine. It just doesn't cut it for my schoolwork and it isn't even good for entertainment. It works but not really that well. It does what I absolutely, bottom-line NEED it to do, but it doesn't do it how I want or expect it to. I would say it's like a splint when what I really need is a cast. In a pinch, it's much better than nothing but it's just not sufficient in the long run.

I find myself constantly frustrated with the poor WiFi connectivity and the slow performance. I added in an SD memory card, but the system does not use it to boost the working memory. It treats it mostly as a memory transfer mechanism, much like a USB memory stick.

Excellent budget laptop with great upgrade potential.

If you don't intend to do any upgrades, you may want to keep looking because this laptop will perform on par with other value laptops in its price range and will underperform desktops in its price range.

However, what makes this laptop a great deal is that it has an open M2 slot (and open RAM slot). Just add a
B+M keyed SATA SSD (I had great luck with the Crucial CT275MX300SSD4) and a 4GB 2400 260-pin DDR 4 SODIMM (I went with CT4G4SFS824A) and the performance really opens up as expected from a machine with SSD drive performance and dual-channel RAM. If you are lucky, your system will arrive with a screw and standoff installed for the M2 drive. Otherwise you will have to locate a screw that fits (2.5mm(?) short) and possibly make a standoff out of a plastic or nylon sleeve. The hardware installation is fairly quick and easy.

Now the key to success is that you need to clone the 1TB HD to what is probably a much smaller SSD. This is actually an easy and straightforward process if you ignore the misinformation out there and just do the following:
1. Start the computer, and go into the BIOS (hit F2 repeatedly after it turns on) and make sure the 1TB drive is on the bottom of the list for boot order and that the SSD is near the top.
2. Then boot up. Install EASEUS ToDo backup Free on this laptop. You will need a blank cd/dvd or flash drive to "sacrifice" because the Easeus software turns it into boot media.
3. Run the Easeus Todo Backup and choose utilities -> Create boot or emergency media. Don't pick LINUX - pick the other option. Then have it create the boot media on either the CD/DVD or flash drive and let it create and format the boot media.
4. Now choose the "Clone" option. Picking the 1TB drive as the source and the SSD as the destination. Make sure you click the "optimize for ssd" box. The program will then go about cloning the larger drive to the smaller SSD. The program may need to reboot to a dos shell to perform the clone (hence the need for the boot media).
5. After it finishes doing it's thing, just reboot and you should notice that it boots MUCH faster. You are now using the SSD as the boot drive and the 1TB HD is the extra storage drive.

Forget some of the other stuff you may read, such as going into diskmanager to format or installing a partition manager to manually change the existing partitions, or using some of the other cloning utilities that won't really work well in Windows 10. Just follow the steps above. When you are done you may want to download the SSD app from whoever made your SSD in order to make sure you are getting the most performance and longevity from it.

That's it. Enjoy your high-performance budget laptop!

I bought this device direct from Motorola. This is the 3rd phone I've owned in the Motorola G family. The first was the original G7, the second the 2019 version of the Motorola G Power and the third... was this one, the Moto G Power (2021 edition). I expected incremental improvements but I was fundamentally wrong.

The camera continues to suck and its AI is laughable - especially at night. Compared alongside an iPhone XS Max the difference is day-and-night (especially night) with the iPhone taking so much better photos that I eventually dug out my old iPhone 7 to create some context. The iPhone 7 was significantly superior except in terms of native resolution. In particular the iPhones are better at scene composition/lighting and target focusing.

However this wasn't the worst problem. I found the radio reception (voice and LTE) was very marginal and inferior to ALL other Motorola G series phones I've owned to-date. In marginal areas, where the G7 produced crystal clear voice and decent LTE speeds (comparable to the iPhone XS Max) the Moto G Power (2021) was unable to make a voice connect and there was 'no internet' reported (aka no LTE).

So ONE MONTH after I bought the Moto G Power (2021) I wanted rid of it. I thought maybe I could trade-in with Motorola, but no, the phone isn't on their list of applicable trade-ins. I can guess why! So I'm very disappointed with Motorola. I was hoping to trade up to the Motorola One 5g ace, but with no trade-in path for a brand new phone I wasn't going to cough up full price replacing what is essentially a product dud.

I should say that in strong signal areas the Moto G Power (2021) worked fine, both voice and data, so I have to suspect that Motorola made design compromises to extend battery life (which, btw, is superb).

Finally I should add that most of the Motorola phones (at the lower and mid levels) come with Android 10 which is already out-of-date. I suspect this has something to do with memory. The Moto G Power (2021) comes with 4G of RAM but perhaps Android 11 prefers more? Honestly don't know.

So overall this phone has only two strong points. The amazing battery life and the relatively speedy processor (considering it's a low end product). But these can't compensate for a fundamental deficit in radio/data communications. If you want a long battery life I'd recommend you get the 2019 version of this phone which works fine for radio/data and has almost no drawbacks compared to the 2021 version.

This is a very good laptop.  The price for the features you get is remarkable. I bought this for $329.99 and purchased a Crucial MX300 275GB M.2 Drive to add in addition to the 1TB Toshiba HDD this particular machine comes with.  For slightly under $400 I was able to buy both items and build a killer budget laptop.  In terms of build quality, my only complaint was the screen bezels seemed very flimsy.  The keyboard has a great feel and it backlit.  the track pad is actually placed in the proper position; centered with the space bar, not centered with the chassis of the laptop. The speakers are alright, dont expect anything great; i mean no laptop actually has good speakers.  The optical drive was a must for my need and a great addition considering the price of the laptop.  The 1080p screen is surprisingly.... alright I'll put it.  I've seen better but this screen is just fine.  I was quite shocked to be honest when i saw this laptop that it even cam with a 1080p screen.  the newest i3 cabylake 7100 is a great, efficient processor that more than capable for day to day multitasking.  This laptop boasts 12hrs of battery life, and i have to say this is a bit optimistic, but definitely do able.  Realistically though may people could get nine hours a battery under normal usage and having things like keyboard backlighting enabled.  4Gb of ram might scare some people off, but I've found very few people actually know how much ram they actually use.  4Gb is plenty for 99% of people.  I think a lot of people get caught up in the marketing mumbo jumbo for ram and think they actually need more.  Ram is not like storage space on your HDD, if you dont use all you ram, there is no point in having it.  Having extra ram does not make your machine faster. at least with a HDD if you are barely utilizing it maximum capacity you could find things to save to the drive if need be. It is also worth mentioning that this model comes with one open ram Dimm slot so you can add additional ram which a lot of times is cheaper than buying the next highest upgraded model for more ram.  I not thrilled that the battery is not accessible.  You can get to the battery by unscrewing the back of the laptop to access it, but im not sure if it voids and warranties.  the outside of the laptop is a nice textured plastic.  To be honest I cant believe that this laptop is selling at about $330.  This is really a steal. Would recommend to anyone looking for a simple laptop for school, work, emails,or websurfing with great features and an unbeatable price.

This was hands down the best IT purchase I have ever made.  In fact, I'd say this is my favorite possession!  I bought this product in October of 2012 as a replacement to my aging, quite heavy, and quite expensive ($2,000 at the time) business laptop.  The trade-offs in low price, excellent battery life, lightning fast startup/reboot, and portability (light weight) immediately make up for any minor annoyances (or just things that are "different" - which you end up getting used to quickly.)  I use this machine for business communication and occasional personal projects.  I've found an app (even some that work "offline") for everything I need to do (even including high tech tasks like programming, connecting to servers, transferring files, etc.)  The only time I find myself switching to a desktop machine is for graphic design tasks.  (I find the screen too small for the precision needed.)  For me, it's a plus that my documents are stored online.  If my Chromebook is ever stolen or dies my data is retained and I'm only out $250 bucks.  In either of these cases, I wouldn't hesitate to purchase another one.  I am thrilled with how much easier this laptop is to use and maintain than traditional Windows systems.  This is a game changer for individuals and small businesses.
